text: Major government funding for AYUSH research: 1) AYUSH Ministry — Extramural Research (EMR) scheme, Central Sector Scheme. 2) Department of Science and Technology (DST) — SERB grants, INSPIRE. 3) Department of Biotechnology (DBT) — biotechnology research. 4) Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) — lab research. 5) Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) — clinical research. 6) BIRAC — startup and industry projects. Application: typically through online portals, peer review, selection. For AYUSH innovators: explore all relevant schemes; different schemes suit different project stages.

AYUSH Ministry research schemes: 1) Extramural Research (EMR) — project-based funding for AYUSH research. 2) Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS) — collaborative research. 3) Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine (CCRUM). 4) Central Council for Research in Homeopathy (CCRH). 5) Central Council for Research in Siddha (CCRS). 6) Central Council for Research in Yoga & Naturopathy (CCRYN). Focus areas: drug development, standardization, clinical validation, safety studies. Apply through respective council websites.

IP ownership from government-funded research: 1) Generally, IP generated from publicly funded research belongs to the PERFORMING INSTITUTION (not government). 2) Government retains royalty-free license for government purposes. 3) Benefit sharing with principal investigators per institutional policy. 4) March-in rights — government can license if not commercialized. 5) Revenue sharing — typically institution retains 60-70%, remainder to government/inventors. Check specific scheme guidelines for IP terms. For AYUSH: ensure clear agreement on IP before starting funded research.

Technology Development Board (TDB) under DST provides loans for commercializing Indian technologies: 1) Soft loan at concessional interest. 2) Focus on scaling up proven technologies. 3) Can fund clinical trials, manufacturing facility, market development. 4) Requires Indian ownership of technology/IP. 5) Typical support: Rs 1-15 crore. For AYUSH: if you have validated formulation/process and need funding for commercialization, TDB is an option. Apply with detailed project proposal and business plan.

Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) supports biotech/pharma innovation: 1) BIG (Biotechnology Ignition Grant) — Rs 50 lakh for startups (proof of concept). 2) SBIRI/BIPP — industry-linked product development. 3) SPARSH — social enterprise support. 4) SEED Fund — prototype development. 5) LEAP — later-stage clinical trials. For AYUSH: biotech-based AYUSH innovations (phytochemistry, novel delivery, biomarkers) eligible. Apply through BIRAC portal with detailed proposal.

Models for AYUSH industry-academia collaboration: 1) Sponsored research — company funds specific project, owns IP. 2) Collaborative research — shared funding, shared IP. 3) Consultancy — institution provides expertise, IP stays with company. 4) Contract research — institution as service provider. 5) Technology licensing — company licenses existing institutional IP. Key document: Research Agreement specifying scope, funding, IP ownership, confidentiality, publication rights. For AYUSH companies: academia provides credibility and research capacity; structure agreements carefully.

Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) recognition provides benefits: 1) In-house R&D recognition — weighted tax deduction on R&D expenses. 2) Customs duty exemption on imported R&D equipment. 3) Excise duty exemption on indigenous equipment. 4) DSIR approved R&D centers can receive government grants. Requirements: dedicated R&D facility, qualified staff, ongoing projects, R&D expenditure. For AYUSH companies: get DSIR recognition for tax benefits and credibility. Maintain proper R&D documentation.

Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) under NITI Aayog supports innovation ecosystem: 1) Atal Incubation Centers — incubation support. 2) Atal New India Challenge — innovation challenges with prizes. 3) Mentor India — connecting innovators with mentors. 4) Atal Community Innovation Centers — grassroots innovation. For AYUSH: apply to Atal Incubation Centers for startup support, participate in relevant innovation challenges. AIM provides non-dilutive funding and ecosystem support.

International funding opportunities for AYUSH: 1) WHO Traditional Medicine programs. 2) NIH (USA) — some grants open to international researchers. 3) EU Horizon programs — collaborative research. 4) Indo-German, Indo-Japan bilateral S&T programs. 5) Wellcome Trust, Gates Foundation — specific disease focus. 6) Industry collaborations with multinational pharma. Challenges: competitive, often require international partnerships, IP terms vary. For AYUSH: international grants bring credibility but read IP clauses carefully — some require royalty-free licensing.

Managing IP from AYUSH research: 1) Patent potentially patentable inventions BEFORE publication. 2) Use lab notebooks and invention disclosure forms. 3) Sign NDAs with collaborators before sharing results. 4) Train researchers on IP awareness. 5) Have institutional IP policy. 6) Work with technology transfer office. Timeline: invention → disclosure → evaluation → patent decision → filing → publication. Timing critical: publication before filing destroys novelty. For AYUSH researchers: coordinate publication plans with patent filing strategy.

AYUSH startup ecosystem: 1) Ministry of AYUSH incubation support. 2) BIRAC BioNEST incubators with AYUSH focus. 3) AYUSH Startup Challenge — annual competition. 4) State-level incubators (Kerala, Karnataka strong for AYUSH). 5) Private incubators (Venture Center, IKP Eden). Benefits: mentorship, seed funding, infrastructure, regulatory guidance, investor access. For AYUSH entrepreneurs: join incubator early, leverage ecosystem support, protect IP proactively. Incubator affiliation adds credibility.
